candidate.answerReason: The phrase 'the two roots' presupposes a genuine quadratic, requiring a(b-c)≠0. In that setting the polynomial factors as (x-1)(a(b-c)x-c(a-b)), giving D. The two roots may coincide.

methods.label: Expose the factor x-1
methods.explanation:
Work in the quadratic setting indicated by “the two roots,” so assume \(a(b-c)\ne0\). The roots need not be distinct. Set
\[
p=a(b-c),\qquad q=c(a-b).
\]
The coefficient identity
\[
a(b-c)+b(c-a)+c(a-b)=0
\]
shows that the coefficient of \(x\) is \(-(p+q)\). This lets us group terms to expose the known root \(1\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
p x^2-(p+q)x+q
&=p x(x-1)-q(x-1)\\
&=(x-1)(p x-q).
\end{aligned}
\]
A product is zero when at least one factor is zero. Thus the roots are \(1\) and \(q/p\), with division valid because \(p\ne0\). If \(q=p\), both roots are \(1\); if \(q=0\), the other root is \(0\).

The nonzero-leading-coefficient condition matters. If \(p=0\), the equation becomes \(q(1-x)=0\): it has only the root \(1\) when \(q\ne0\), and every \(x\) satisfies it when \(q=0\). Those are not two-root quadratic cases. In the stated quadratic setting, the other root is therefore
\[
\boxed{\frac{c(a-b)}{a(b-c)}},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).

candidate.annotationRationale: The target is recovering a quadratic root from the coefficients and a known root. The written method derives this relationship by grouping and factoring, rather than invoking a memorized formula. Quadratic classification supplies the nonzero-leading-coefficient condition; no polynomial division or quadratic formula is needed.
limitations: The quadratic setting presupposes a(b-c)≠0, although that restriction is not displayed separately. Degenerate choices give a linear equation or an identity, not a uniquely defined second quadratic root.
The other root may equal 1; distinctness is not required.

review.mathematicalCheck: The coefficient sum vanishes identically, and the polynomial equals (x-1)(px-q), where p=a(b-c) and q=c(a-b). For p≠0 the other root is q/p, including multiplicities. For p=0, the stated linear and identity cases are correct.
